front.title: Owner Policy, Assurance and Attention for User-Managed Access (UMA) 2.0

abstract.t: This document specifies what a resource owner's policy over autonomous agents may say, what may be known about an agent before the owner has met it, and how the owner's attention is defended.

Its central rule is an asymmetry: evidence supplied by the requesting side may only tighten a requirement, and only the owner's own prior decisions may relax one. Agent assurance is decomposed into three independent axes with no composite score. Once the owner has met an agent, how much it may do without asking her is an earned level that only she raises, kept apart from the level its operator declares, which may only tighten. The owner's pending queue has a depth limit, in two lanes, so that a party who can mint keys for free cannot make "the owner decides" into a denial of service. And the owner's record of what was promised, decided and done names the counterparty on every row it honestly can.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: lets a resource owner's authorization server decide on her behalf and says nothing about what the policy it decides from may contain. That was the right silence for a specification meant to be profiled, and this document is one such profile.

The policy an owner writes over agents differs from the policy an administrator writes over users in one respect that changes everything: the party being decided about supplies most of the evidence. An agent presents its own key, its own operator's name, its own credential from its own issuer. A rule that widens access when that evidence looks good is a rule the agent can satisfy by producing the evidence. This document exists mainly to say, once and structurally, that such a rule must not be storable.

section.name: Relationship to the Set
section.t: This document is an OPTIONAL extension of and depends on . Its identifying URI is https://u4a.ai/spec/policy/1.0.

section.name: Notational Conventions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: The Shape of a Policy
section.t: An owner's policy is written against resources, not against agents. Each policy unit MUST name the resources it covers, MUST name the terms proffered for them (see ), MUST state whether the owner is asked before access is granted, and MAY carry rules.
A resource MUST belong to exactly one policy unit. A resource that belongs to none is ungoverned, and an authorization server MUST refuse access to an ungoverned resource rather than apply a default.

A rule is a list of conditions and an effect. The conditions of one rule are conjoined; the rules of one unit are disjoined; and an implementation MUST NOT offer negation, nesting, or expressions. This is a small, legible document, not a policy language: the owner reads it, and a policy she cannot read is a policy she did not write.

figure.title: A unit that asks, except for an agent of ninety days' unbroken standing, unless nobody stands behind it.

section.t: The effects are auto, ask and refuse, in increasing order of strictness. ask_me is the unit's baseline: ask where true, auto where false.

section.name: The Asymmetry
section.t: Every condition a rule may name is classed as either relaxing or observed.

A relaxing condition is a fact that traces to a decision the owner personally made about this agent, or to a check the owner's authority ran on the owner's own published material. An observed condition is anything else: what the requesting side presented, what its operator published, what this server did automatically, and what the owner did in aggregate.

A rule whose effect is auto MUST name only relaxing conditions. An authorization server MUST refuse to store a rule that would relax a requirement on an observed condition, and MUST refuse it at the moment the owner attempts to save it rather than storing it and ignoring it at evaluation time.

Enforcing this where policy is stored, rather than where it is evaluated, is the difference between a deployment that cannot express the mistake and one that believes it has a control it does not have.

section.name: What May Relax
section.t: An implementation MUST NOT class any condition as relaxing unless it is one of the following kinds, and MUST class every one of the following as relaxing if it offers it:

list.t: the owner personally approved access for this agent at this policy unit;
the owner has never revoked this agent;
the owner's relationship with this agent is older than a stated duration;
the agent is one the owner activated herself, as ;
the owner has raised this agent to at least a stated level of her own autonomy ladder, as .

section.t: "The owner has previously granted here" is not on the list, and the distinction is the point. A grant this server made may have been automatic, and relaxing on it lets one automatic grant justify the next. What may safely relax is what the owner herself decided. An implementation MUST keep the record of grants it made and the record of approvals the owner gave apart, and MUST NOT write an approval where the decision was taken by someone acting for her (see ).

An authorization server MUST record who made a decision in the same step that records the decision, and MUST NOT write an approval as the owner's unless that record names her. Written in two steps, the moment between them holds a decision with no author, and a grant loop reading it then has nothing to tell her approval from an administrator's.

A recorded decision MUST NOT be undone by a later write of the negotiation it decides. The writer is routinely holding a copy read before the decision was made — the client's poll rotating its ticket — and writing that copy back would put a request she has answered back in front of her.

section.name: What May Only Tighten
section.t: Every other condition may appear only in a rule whose effect is ask or refuse. This includes, without limit:

list.t: the agent's assurance on any axis of ;
the absence of a stated reason or cited mission in the agreement ();
that the agent was introduced by another agent ();
that the agent stands below a stated level of the owner's autonomy ladder, or of its operator's (), or that its operator declares none.

section.t: A rule that tightens on the owner's own aggregate conduct — "she has denied this agent four times" — reads the owner's decisions and is still observed rather than relaxing, because "she has denied you repeatedly, so grant automatically" is not a sentence anyone should be able to save.

section.name: Declared Consequence
section.t: A resource server may declare what an operation leaves behind, as specifies: reversible, compensatable, forward_recoverable or irreversible, ordered by how much remedy remains after the act. An authorization server MAY offer conditions naming that declaration, so that an owner can write "ask me about anything that cannot be undone" without naming a tool — a rule that holds for operations she has never seen, at resource servers she has never heard of.

An authorization server offering such a condition MUST treat it as one that may only tighten, under . The declaration is made by the resource server rather than by the requesting party, which is what makes it readable at all; it is still a fact about the request rather than a decision of the owner's, and only her own decisions relax anything.

An authorization server MUST NOT treat an operation carrying no declaration as satisfying a condition about how much remedy remains. It MAY offer a separate condition that names the absence itself, so that an owner who wishes to refuse what nobody will describe can say so. The two are different sentences: one is about an act that cannot be undone, the other about an act nobody has described, and an owner is entitled to hold different opinions of them.

The order is by remedy and not by severity. An authorization server MUST NOT present it to an owner as a measure of harm, and MUST NOT combine it with the axes of into a single score: a reversible act may still be catastrophic while it stands, and a composite is the mechanism by which one reading quietly excuses another.

section.name: Clearance
section.t: Some authorizations are not the owner's to give. Whether an act is lawful for the party behind it — a licence that is current, a jurisdiction where the act is permitted — is a fact about the world, established by somebody else, and the owner's terms cannot settle it.

A policy unit MAY require such facts. A requirement is a set of claims, each naming the values that satisfy it. Where a layer above the owner requires clearance as well (), the two MUST be combined by intersection: a claim either requires is required, and a claim both require is satisfied only by values both accept. The layer above may add a claim and narrow an accepted value, and MUST NOT remove a requirement the owner wrote.

An authorization server MUST obtain a clearance from the attesting party the policy names, and MUST NOT accept one presented by the client as a claim token. The rule is the one arrives at for verdicts, from the other direction: a claim works when the requesting party is the only one who holds the fact, and fails when the fact may be adverse to it. A licence is adverse-capable — its holder has every reason to say it is current — so the attestation travels from the attesting party to the authorization server directly.

Where the attesting party is the organization the owner enrolled with, her authorization server fetches the attestation from the organization's clearance_endpoint with her membership credential (). It is a JWT with typ of u4a-clearance+jwt, signed with a key at the attesting party's jwks_uri, carrying iss, sub (the owner, as her authorization server names her), aud (her authorization server's issuer identifier), iat, exp, jti, and clearance: an object whose members are the attested claims and whose values are the attested values.

An authorization server MUST verify the attestation's signature against keys the attesting party publishes, and MUST refuse it unless it names the subject the negotiation is about and names that authorization server as its audience. An attestation about one member, issued to one authority, is not evidence about another member or at another authority.
The digest a grant carries ( Section 7.1) is s256 over the serialization of that clearance object, as verified.

Where a required clearance is unmet, an authorization server MUST refuse the negotiation before it dictates terms, and MUST record the reason. An agent that signed an agreement it was never going to be allowed to act under would hold a record of a bargain that never existed, and the owner's record would carry an undertaking that decided nothing.

An authorization server that cannot reach the attesting party has no attestation, and so refuses under the rule above. A party that cannot be reached has not attested to anything, and the direction to fail in is the one the ceiling of already fails in.

section.name: Evaluation Order
section.t: An authorization server MUST evaluate a policy unit's rules in two passes: first every rule whose effect is auto, then every rule whose effect is stricter than the running result. A restriction that matches MUST win over a relaxation that also matched, whatever order the rules were written in.

The running result starts at the unit's baseline. A matching auto rule in the first pass sets it to auto, which is how an owner lets some requests through a unit that otherwise asks; on a unit whose baseline is already auto, an auto rule changes nothing.

A rule that cannot be evaluated — because a fact or condition it names is absent, unknown or malformed — MUST be treated as matching if its effect is ask or refuse and as not matching if its effect is auto. Both land on more friction. The alternative treats a broken restriction as a working one and a broken relaxation as a refusal, and the first of those is the one an owner would not choose.

Until a client holds a standing connection with the owner, a matching rule whose effect is refuse is the only outcome of evaluation an authorization server may act on. It MUST otherwise put the first contact to the owner, whatever the rules would decide, and MUST record a refusal made in its place as describes. A rule may turn away a client the owner has not met; no rule may admit one.

section.name: Publication
section.t: An authorization server MUST publish the conditions its rules may name, and for each MUST state whether it may relax. The owner's editing surface then teaches the rule at the moment it matters, rather than rejecting a save the owner has already composed.

section.name: Three Axes
section.t: What an authorization server may know about an agent before the owner has met it decomposes on three independent axes. An implementation MUST derive each from a check that has run and passed, MUST NOT accept any of them from the requesting side's own assertion, and MUST NOT combine them into a single score.

dd.t: Whether the agreement's signature verified against a key this authority can name. Level 0: no. Level 1: yes.
Whether the agent's credential traces to an issuer whose keys this authority fetched. Level 0: the agent is pseudonymous. Level 1: an issuer vouched for it.

Whether anyone named and reachable stands behind the agent. Level 0: nobody. Level 1: the agent named a client metadata document that resolved and claims its own URL. Level 2: the operator — the origin of that document's client_id — publishes, in the key directory named by the agreement's signature_agent header member at that same origin, the JWK thumbprint of the key that signed the agreement.

section.t: The decomposition follows the same reasoning as the separation of identity, authentication and federation assurance in : a composite is the mechanism by which strong key binding excuses an unknown operator, which is a trade nobody would make if asked directly.

section.name: Level 2 Is the Only Level an Agent Cannot Reach Alone
section.t: A metadata document proves that it claims its own URL; anyone can publish one, so level 1 on the accountability axis is available to any agent that wants it. Level 2 requires that the key directory be at the same origin as the metadata document, so that an agent cannot point at a directory it runs itself, and it requires the directory to hold the specific key that signed. Only the operator can put a key there.

A directory that cannot be resolved MUST leave the agent at level 1, not level 0. An operator's outage is not evidence about an agent. An implementation MUST cache a directory hit and MUST NOT cache a miss, since a stale hit merely keeps attesting a key the operator has disowned for the cache's lifetime, and a stale miss fails to recognise a key the operator just published for the same lifetime — and only the first of those is bounded by something the operator controls.

section.name: Assurance Is Not a Gate
section.t: Assurance MUST NOT decide admission. An agent at level 0 on every axis is admitted to negotiation like any other stranger, and the owner is asked. What assurance does is give the owner's rules something true to tighten on, and give the attention budget of a lane.

A lie can only cost the liar friction. An agent that claims an operator it does not belong to gains nothing, because the claim never widens anything; it loses the attributable lane and the owner's trust.

section.name: The Owner's Own Agent
section.t: An agent the owner activated herself is the one case where the requesting party and the resource owner are the same person. This document does not specify it as a special case, because a profile that has to branch on it is telling you its party model is wrong. Terms, grant and enforcement are byte-identical; what the case needs is one policy condition.

An authorization server MUST let the owner claim an operator origin as her own, and MUST class an agent as the owner's own only where both hold: the operator it names, the origin of its client_id, is one she has claimed, and that operator's key directory publishes the key that signed. The first half is her decision; the second is a check her authority ran on material only the operator controls. Neither is anything the requesting side can assert.
This condition MAY relax a rule (see ). It MUST NOT skip first contact, and it MUST NOT beat a restriction that also matched.
The owner MUST be able to disclaim an origin. Disclaiming takes effect on the next request and revokes nothing; the claim bought friction, not access.

section.name: A Depth Limit, Not a Rate Limit
section.t: Keys are free. An unbounded pending queue turns "the owner decides" into a denial-of-service surface, and every request in the flood is individually well-formed. A rate limit does not express the constraint: the scarce thing is how many questions the owner can be made to hold, not how fast they arrive.

An authorization server MUST bound the number of pending requests from agents that hold no standing connection. Past the bound it MUST refuse with 429 and error of request_denied, and MUST NOT queue. An agent that holds an active connection MUST NOT be counted against the bound and MUST NOT be refused for it, unless it holds that connection by introduction ( Section 5): an introduced agent skipped the owner's first question, not her queue, and is counted as a first contact would be.

Section 3.3.6 answers request_denied with 403. The bound uses 429 because the refusal reports the state of the owner's queue rather than a decision about the request, and a client should not read it as one.

section.name: Two Lanes
section.t: The bound MUST be applied in two lanes, split on whether the agent is at level 2 on the accountability axis. Each lane has its own depth, and an implementation SHOULD set the attributable lane deeper.

The agent the owner wants to admit is a stranger too on first contact. A single queue defends continuity and leaves onboarding undefended: one anonymous flood and the agent she is expecting cannot reach her. Two lanes let a flood of strangers fill the lane strangers use, while an agent whose operator has published its key still gets through. The lane boundary is level 2 because it is the only level an agent cannot reach on its own say-so ().

section.name: Blocking
section.t: The owner MUST be able to block an operator by origin. Blocking MUST end every active connection held by an agent of that operator and MUST invalidate the grants under them, in one step, and MUST cause future requests naming that operator to be refused before the owner's policy is evaluated.
Blocking is a restriction, so it MAY rest on the agent's own claim of its operator: an agent that misstates its operator only refuses itself.
Unblocking MUST NOT restore connections that blocking ended. It restores the right to negotiate, not the access that was withdrawn.

section.name: The Limit
section.t: Blocking does not remove a party from the network. The same operator may drop its client identifier and return as an anonymous stranger — in the unattributable lane, with nothing standing behind it. That is the honest limit of operator-level refusal, and it is why the lanes of matter more than the block does.

section.name: The Record
section.t: An authorization server implementing this document keeps an append-only record of what was promised, decided, done and withdrawn, and the following are requirements on it.

section.name: One Correlation Identifier
section.t: An authorization server MUST assign the identifier of a negotiation once, when the permission ticket is first created, and MUST carry it unchanged through every ticket rotation. The ticket is a credential for the negotiation; the negotiation is the thing the record is about.

section.name: Refusals Are Recorded
section.t: An authorization server MUST record a refusal — by policy, by a blocked operator, by the attention bound, or by the owner — with the same prominence as a grant. A record that shows only successes is indistinguishable from a deployment with enforcement switched off.

section.name: The Row Names the Counterparty
section.t: Every entry in the record that concerns a client MUST carry that client's connection handle as an indexed attribute of the row, and MUST do so for refusals and denials as well as grants. A denied negotiation issues no token, so nothing downstream links that entry to an agent; if the row does not carry the handle, the question owners most want answered — this agent has asked four times and I have said no four times — cannot be derived from what was stored.

Exactly one class of entry cannot carry a handle: a refusal by the requesting side that arrives before it has signed anything (). An authorization server MUST record such an entry without an attribution rather than invent one.

section.name: Not the Owner's Decision
section.t: Where a decision was taken by someone acting for the owner, the record MUST say who, and the decision MUST NOT be written as the owner's. This is the requirement that keeps honest: "the owner personally approved" is allowed to relax a rule, so a decision taken on her behalf must not produce that fact.

section.name: Enforcement Point Reports Do Not Carry the Handle
section.t: Where an enforcement point reports an allowed call to the authorization server, the authorization server MUST resolve the agent from the negotiation and MUST NOT accept a handle from the report. The enforcement point is the resource server's component; which agent did what is the owner's record and not the resource server's to assert.

section.name: Earned Autonomy
section.t: says what an authorization server may know about an agent before the owner has met it. This section says how much an agent she has met may do without asking her, and how the owner raises that over time.

The vocabulary is the maturity model of the Agentic Trust Framework . Four levels, in increasing order of what an agent may do unsupervised: intern (observes and reports), junior (may act, every act approved first), senior (acts, and a person is told), principal (acts within an approved domain, and escalates the edge). describes these as one ladder, climbed by an agent as the organization that deploys it comes to trust it. Inside one organization that is the whole picture: the party governing the agent and the party whose systems it reaches are the same party.

Under this profile they are not. The agent's operator runs it on behalf of a requesting party; the resource owner holds what it asks for. So every agent stands on two ladders at once: the one its operator keeps, and the one the owner keeps. They answer different questions — how far does the party running this agent trust it, and how far does this owner — and an answer to the first is evidence about the second only in one direction.

section.name: Two Ladders
section.t: An authorization server implementing this section MUST keep the level the owner has given an agent and the level the agent's operator declares as two facts, and MUST NOT combine them into a single level. An owner's rules read each through its own conditions.

The reason is the one gives for refusing a composite assurance score. A combined level is the mechanism by which an operator's confidence in its own agent would come to stand in for an owner's, and that is a trade no owner would make if asked directly. Whichever ladder stands lower is the one that governs, and an owner who wants that writes it as rules ().

section.name: The Owner's Ladder
section.t: An authorization server keeps one level per standing connection. An agent with no standing connection MUST be treated as at the lowest level, and a connection the owner admits, including one she readmits after revoking it, MUST begin there. A level granted by another party, an operator's included, is not standing with her.

An authorization server MUST NOT raise an agent's level except on the owner's own decision, and MUST NOT raise it on a decision taken on her behalf (). It MUST NOT raise a level by more than one step in one decision: the time an agent spends at each level is the only evidence of its conduct there that the owner will ever have, and skipping a level discards it. The owner MUST be able to lower an agent's level by any number of steps in one decision, and revoking the agent lowers it to the bottom.

Together these give the property that lets the level relax a rule (): it can rise only by the owner's hand, one step at a time, so whatever it reads is at or below a level she personally granted. A condition that the agent stands at least at the lowest level holds for every agent, including one the owner has never met, and MUST be refused where the rule is stored ().

Two parties may move one agent's level without seeing each other — the owner from a view she opened a minute ago, and a second surface or a second authorization server acting on something newer. An authorization server MUST apply a change of level only if the agent still stands at the level the person deciding was shown, so that a stale promotion cannot overwrite a demotion it never saw. It MUST record every change of level, with the level before and after and who decided it, in the record of .

sets five conditions on a promotion: performance, security validation, business value, incident record and governance sign-off. An authorization server SHOULD show the owner, beside the decision, what her own record says about the first and fourth — how long the agent has stood at its level, how often she approved what it asked there, and whether her policy refused it — and SHOULD say that the second and third are evidence about the operator's programme rather than about this agent with her. The fifth is her decision itself. Nothing an authorization server computes from these may promote an agent.

A refusal is evidence about the agent's conduct only when her policy refused the request on its own merits. A refusal because of where the agent stands on either ladder is the ladder working, and a refusal because the owner's queue was full () is about the owner; neither is an incident.

Evidence from a party outside both — an evaluator's signed appraisal of what the agent has done elsewhere — would belong beside these conditions. It would travel as a clearance does (): fetched by the authorization server from the party that signed it, verified against that party's published keys, bound to this agent, and never carried by the agent itself. Like the rest, it would inform the owner's decision and could not make it. This document does not define its format.

A refusal is evidence about the agent's conduct only when her policy refused the request on its own merits. A refusal because of where the agent stands on either ladder is the ladder working, and a refusal because the owner's queue was full () is about the owner; neither is an incident.

Evidence from a party outside both — an evaluator's signed appraisal of what the agent has done elsewhere — would belong beside these conditions. It would travel as a clearance does (): fetched by the authorization server from the party that signed it, verified against that party's published keys, bound to this agent, and never carried by the agent itself. Like the rest, it would inform the owner's decision and could not make it. This document does not define its format.

section.name: The Operator's Ladder
section.t: An operator declares where it has put an agent on its own ladder in the client metadata document the agent names, as a member atf whose value is an object:

figure.title: An operator's declaration of its agent's level, in its client metadata document.

section.t: maturity_level is one of the four levels; conformance is compatible or certified in the sense of ; statement_uri locates the operator's conformance statement. A level is per client, so an operator running agents at different levels publishes a document per class of agent.

An authorization server that reads the declaration MUST read it only from a client metadata document that resolved and claims its own URL, and MUST NOT read it from anything the agent itself sent. It MUST treat the operator's level as a condition that may only tighten, under : the declaration is the requesting side's statement about itself, and a level it raises reaches nobody's resources. An operator that declares no level MUST NOT satisfy a condition that its level is below a stated level; an operator that has not heard of is not saying its agent is an intern. An authorization server MAY offer a separate condition naming the absence.

Because it may only tighten, the declaration needs no verification to be safe to read: an operator that overstates its agent gains nothing, and one that understates it costs only itself. It is shown to the owner with what the authorization server could establish about who made it — an operator at level 2 of the accountability axis (), or a document any agent could have named.

An operator lowering its agent is the change that must reach the owner, since a stale copy of the document goes on reading the level from before. An authorization server MUST bound how long it relies on a copy of a client metadata document from which it reads a level, and SHOULD use the same bound as for an operator's key directory.

A declaration of certified is the operator's claim that a third party audited its programme. An authorization server MUST NOT treat it as an attestation, and MUST NOT raise any axis of on it. Third-party attestation is the evidence that would let somebody outside the operator stand behind its ladder, and it would belong on the accountability axis, above level 2; it needs a party a relying authorization server can ask, which does not yet define.

section.name: Acting Without Asking
section.t: The senior level of is "act and notify". Where a grant is issued without asking the owner for an operation whose declared consequence is compensatable or worse, or because a rule relaxed a unit that would otherwise have asked, the authorization server SHOULD tell the owner as it happens, on whatever surface would otherwise have asked her. A relaxation is also recorded ().

section.t: The operator's ladder is then read the same way and can only make a cell stricter: an agent its operator still calls an intern does not act on her resources however far she has promoted it. The only rule in the profile that relaxes anything reads the owner's own decision.

An operation no resource server has described is put to the owner when an intern asks for it rather than refused, because an undescribed read is common and refusing it would make the profile unusable on most resources.

section.name: Containment
section.t: A policy unit's terms MAY state a call rate: a number of calls and a period. An authorization server that offers one MUST refuse at introspection a grant whose agent has already made that many calls at that unit within the period, with error of rate_limited, counting only calls an enforcement point reported as allowed. Because the rate is in the terms, the agent agrees to it before it holds a grant.

An enforcement point SHOULD report a call it refused after the agent's signature verified, and the authorization server records it against the agent as it does an allowed call (). Refusals before the signature verified are not counted, since anyone holding a copy of a grant could cause them. An authorization server MAY suspend an agent after a number of such refusals within a window. A suspension MUST stop every grant the agent holds and every new grant, with error of suspended, and MUST lower the agent to the bottom of the owner's ladder (). It MUST NOT be lifted by anyone but the owner. It keeps the connection and the rest of the agent's standing.
Both rate_limited and suspended are terminal in the sense of Section 5: a fresh negotiation cannot change either.

section.name: The Asymmetry Is the Security Model
section.t: Everything else in this document follows from . A deployment that lets an observed condition relax a rule has let the party being decided about write the decision, and the mechanism by which it did so — a well-formed key, a resolvable document, an operator's name — costs that party nothing.

section.name: Assurance Is Derived, Never Claimed
section.t: An implementation that reads an assurance level from anything the requesting side sent has reintroduced the problem exists to remove. Each level is the result of a check this authority ran, and the check either ran and passed or the level is zero.

section.name: Promotion Is a Relaxation
section.t: Raising an agent on the owner's ladder widens what it may do at every policy unit that reads the ladder, from that request onward. That is why only the owner may do it, one step at a time, and why the write is conditional on the level she was shown (). An implementation that let an administrator, an operator, or an automatic process raise the level would have built the relaxation exists to forbid, under a different name.
Lowering needs none of this. A demotion, by anyone and by any distance, can only make the owner's rules stricter.

section.name: Trajectory Reads Are Not Atomic
section.t: The conditions of that read the owner's recent record — denials, policy units asked at, calls made — need not be read atomically. A count that only ever tightens is monotone inside its window: a stale read behaves as an earlier arrival would have, and cannot widen access beyond what a differently timed arrival would have received. The test for whether a read needs the indivisibility of Section 8.3 is whether staleness can widen; these cannot.

section.name: The Bound Is a Depth, and the Depth Is Small
section.t: An implementation SHOULD default the unattributable lane to a single-digit depth. The cost of a bound set too low is that a legitimate stranger is told to try later; the cost of one set too high is an owner who cannot find the request she is waiting for.

section.name: The Record Is a Per-Agent History
section.t: makes the record queryable by agent, which is what the owner needs and is also a history of one party's requests kept by another. Retention is deployment policy. An implementation SHOULD let the owner see every entry that names an agent, since she is the party it was kept for.

section.name: Operator Claims Are Visible to the Owner
section.t: An agent's claimed operator is shown to the owner whether or not it verifies, with the level it reached. An implementation MUST make the difference visible — "named" and "published this agent's key" are different sentences — because a resolved name is exactly what an owner starts keying decisions on, and is the only level that means what it appears to.

section.name: An Operator's Level Is Shown, Not Hidden
section.t: The operator's declared level is shown to the owner alongside her own, as two statements. It is information the operator chose to publish about its own agent; nothing about the owner is disclosed to the operator by reading it.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document makes no request of IANA. The conditions of and are described by kind rather than by name so that an implementation may name them in its own vocabulary; records one such vocabulary without registering it.

abstract.t: This specification defines a method for computing a hash value over a JSON Web Key (JWK). It defines which fields in a JWK are used in the hash computation, the method of creating a canonical form for those fields, and how to convert the resulting Unicode string into a byte sequence to be hashed. The resulting hash value can be used for identifying or selecting the key represented by the JWK that is the subject of the thumbprint.

Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably repeatable. One way to address this is to create a canonical representation of the data. Canonicalization also permits data to be exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.

This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property sorting.

front.title: Registry and Signature Agent card for Web bot auth

abstract.t: This document defines the "Signature Agent Card", a JSON metadata document that a signature agent using [DIRECTORY] publishes to describe itself: its identity, purpose, rate expectations, and cryptographic keys. Its parameters are drawn from the OAuth Dynamic Client Registration Metadata registry [DCR], the same namespace used by [CIMD], extended with a single web_bot_auth object. This document registers that object with IANA and establishes a registry for its members.

This specification defines a mechanism through which an OAuth client can identify itself to authorization servers, without prior dynamic client registration or other existing registration. This is through the usage of a URL as a client_id in an OAuth flow, where the URL refers to a document containing the necessary client metadata, enabling the authorization server to fetch the metadata about the client as needed.

Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

section.name: Mapping to the Agentic Trust Framework
section.t: This appendix is not normative. sets 25 requirements across five elements for an organization deploying agents. Under this profile some fall to the operator, as assumes, and some are met by the resource owner's authorization server on her side of the exchange, which is the side does not describe.
Each requirement is given one of four statuses, judged only for requests that reach the owner's resources:

texttable.title: ATF's requirements, judged on the owner's side of the exchange.
texttable.c: The connection handle names each agent to the owner: its key's thumbprint, or its issuer and subject ().
Every agreement and call is signed with the agent's key; the binding axis records it ().
The accountability axis names the operator, and level 2 is the operator's own attestation (). The chain from the operator to the person it acts for is not established.
Each agreement carries the purpose the owner's terms state and the agent's reason (). This is per grant; a standing declaration of the agent's scope is the operator's.
The record of , for everything that reaches her resources.
Every row of the record names the agent where it can (); an enforcement point's report is attributed by the authorization server, not the reporter ().
The trajectory conditions of count denials, units and calls in a window. They are not a baseline.
A rule can tighten when an agent's requests widen or multiply (). There is no detection beyond such counts.
The conditions that decided each request are kept in the record. The agent's own rationale is only its stated reason, which nothing checks.
Her side validates the agreement against her terms and the call against the operation it was granted for; the agent's inputs are not hers to see.
Not detected. Per-operation grants bound what an injected instruction can do on her resources.
Scopes limit what is released, and her terms prohibit uses of it. Detection and masking are the operator's, and most prohibitions are undertakings rather than enforced ().
The record links what an agent promised to what it touched, per negotiation, and sub-agents to the agent that introduced them (). Lineage inside the agent's pipeline is the operator's.
Each policy unit names its resources; an ungoverned resource is refused ().
Scopes per unit, and grants bound to one named operation ().
A call rate in the terms of a policy unit, enforced at introspection ().
A grant may be bound to one operation and its parameters and spent once (); terms may carry constraints.
Access is per unit, an operator can be blocked in one action (), and revoking an agent revokes its lineage (). Cumulative impact across calls is not limited.
Repeated calls refused after the agent's signature verified suspend it until the owner lifts the suspension ().
Revoking a connection or blocking an operator takes effect on the next call, because the enforcement point introspects every call. It stops access, not the agent.
Revoking a connection deactivates every grant issued under it in one step ().
Undoing an act is the resource server's. The declared consequence of says whether it can be undone, and the owner's rules read it.
Lowering either ladder takes effect on the agent's next request ().

Its automatic demotion triggers — a critical incident, a discovered vulnerability, repeated minor incidents — are observed by the operator, which is where places them, and reach every owner through the operator's ladder on the agent's next request without any owner acting.

section.t: The decomposition of follows . The operator key directory of and the client metadata document of are what make the accountability axis derivable rather than asserted.
The levels of are those of the Agentic Trust Framework .

The consequence vocabulary of — reversible, compensatable, forward-recoverable, irreversible — is Nat Sakimura's, from "When Software Becomes Staff: Governance, Security & Safety for Agentic AI" (https://nat.sakimura.org/2026/05/19/when-software-becomes-staff-governance-security-safety-for-agentic-ai/). That work also states the objection this document answers structurally: a capability an agent declares about itself is advertising, so the declaration here is made by the resource and read by the party that bears the cost.
